newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Turkish premier seeks closer ties with Libya.
newsitem.headline: Turkish premier seeks closer ties with Libya.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, making a visit to Libya that has stirred controversy both in Turkey and among its Western allies, was quoted on Saturday as saying he wanted closer ties with Tripoli.

The official Libyan news agency JANA reported that Erbakan, on arrival on Friday night, reiterated his government's rejection of U.N. sanctions imposed on Libya for its refusal to hand over two Libyans suspected of blowing up a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland in 1988.
"This visit is a start for strong and solid ties and will expand fields of trade cooperation between our two countries," he was quoted as saying.
Turkey's Anatolian news agency also quoted Erbakan as saying his trip would be a "starting point" for closer cooperation between the two countries.
Erbakan flew from Cairo to the Tunisian island of Jerba and then travelled by road across the border to Tripoli, a Turkish diplomat in Tunis said.
He cannot fly straight to Libya because of the sanctions.

"Our government rejects the injust sanctions imposed on Libya, and we have experienced by ourselves the lack of credibility of these measures. We were to fly straight to Tripoli, but we were forced to take several roads," Erbakan said, quoted by JANA.
Anatolian news agency quoted Erbakan as saying Libya could sell Turkey oil, natural gas, petrochemicals and fertiliser and buy food, textiles and industrial products.
Erbakan leads a 120-strong delegation including businessmen and members of parliament from all political parties, Turkish diplomats said.

Turkish Energy Minister Recai Kutan started talks with Libyan officials on Wednesday on economic and energy cooperation. Turkish officials want Libya to repay debts of up to $365 million due to Turkish contractors.

Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, the Islamists' conservative coalition partner, has described the visit as ill-timed and the interior minister, a member of Ciller's party, has threatened to resign over the trip.
Washington, already wary of modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, has expressed its own disquiet.
Few foreign leaders have visited Tripoli since the United Nations imposed an air and limited trade embargo on Libya.

Erbakan has also visited Iran since becoming Turkey's first Islamist prime minister in June. The United States accuses both Libya and Iran of sponsoring state terrorism and has rebuked its NATO ally for forging closer ties with the two countries.

"This visit is not aimed against any country or society in the world," Erbakan told reporters before leaving Turkey for Egypt, the first stop on his regional tour. "America is our friend and ally," he added.
But he noted Turkey was a sovereign state and had to look out for its commercial interests. Increased imports of crude oil from Libya and natural gas from Nigeria are also on the agenda.
Erbakan is due to travel from Libya to Nigeria, also rich in natural resources but under fire from the West over the human rights record of its military government.
